newsitem.title: HONG KONG: World hails Deng for opening up China.
newsitem.headline: World hails Deng for opening up China.

text.p: President Bill Clinton and other world leaders paid tribute on Thursday to China's paramount leader Deng Xiaoping, praising him for opening up the world's most populous nation.
Clinton called Deng an "extraordinary figure on the world stage over the past two decades".
Deng died late on Wednesday of respiratory failure. He was 92 and in the advanced stages of Parkinson's disease.

In a statement during a visit to Boston, Clinton expressed his sadness and described Deng as "the driving force behind China's decision to formalise relations with the United States" in the late 1970s.

U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, visiting London, paid tribute to Deng and told reporters: "It would obviously be a great advantage to the Chinese as well as to all of us if there were a smooth transition (in Beijing)."

Reaction in Asian financial markets was generally positive with stocks in China, Hong Kong and Taiwan closing mostly higher as Deng's death was seen as removing recent uncertainties from the markets. It was not a factor in early European trading.

Hong Kong stocks jumped 2.33 percent by the close, or 305.01 points, after an initial loss of 92 points. "Investors feel that the last detectable uncertainty in China has been removed with the death of Deng Xiaoping," said Peter So, deputy head of research at Schroder Securities.
Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said he was greatly saddened, adding "the Japan-China relationship is of growing importance for peace and stability in Asia and the world".
Reactions were mixed among Beijing residents.
"I feel a great sadness," said snack vendor Xie Weicai as he prepared his pavement stove for the morning's business.
But not so for one taxi driver. "I would consider losing 100 yuan ($12) much sadder than the death of Deng Xiaoping," the driver said. "It has nothing to do with me."

It was business as usual on the capital's streets, with residents busy opening shops and crowding on to buses to go to work, in stark contrast to the paralysis that gripped China with the passing of Chairman Mao Zedong in 1976.
French President Jacques Chirac praised the dead Chinese leader as the main architect of China's modernisation.
The office of British Prime Minister John Major said Deng's "initiative played the crucial part in creating today's economically dynamic and successful China".
Germany described Deng as an important statesman who had decisively influenced China's development over 20 years.
"Deng Xiaoping counts as one of the great leadership personalities of China's recent history," Chancellor Helmut Kohl said in a statement, offering his condolences to the Chinese people.

Diplomats at NATO, which has no formal dealings with China, took the death calmly, saying it was not unexpected and unlikely to have any impact in the alliance's main European sphere of influence. There was no official comment from the alliance.
China opposes NATO's plans to expand eastwards, but far less stridently than Moscow. NATO sources said they expected no policy change on that front following Deng's death.

In Hong Kong, Governor Chris Patten described Deng as "an historic figure". Patten is the territory's last governor before it reverts to Chinese sovereignty at midnight on June 30, ending more than 150 years of British colonial rule.

"He will be regarded by future generations as an historic figure. His concept of 'one country, two systems' helped to make possible the successful negotiation of the Joint Declaration, and thus to lay the foundation for Hong Kong's stability and prosperity after 1997," Patten said.
Taiwan's Presidential Office sent its condolences to Deng's family and urged a "peaceful, cooperative, prosperous new era" between Taipei and Beijing.
But the island, which Beijing regards as a renegade province, maintained a military alert and urged calm.

The patriarch's death has long raised fears of a power struggle but diplomats in Beijing said any immediate factional fighting was unlikely in the China's internecine political world because Deng's anointed heir, party chief Jiang Zemin, had a firm grip on power.
Chinese-American activist Harry Wu disagreed and said Deng's death would spark a power struggle and possibly a civil war.

Analysts also saw little immediate change. "There is going to be a lull," said Tai Ming Cheung, an analyst at Kim Eng Securities in Hong Kong. "There may be a certain amount of policy paralysis... but beyond that I don't see any great changes."

Xiao Qiang, the leader of Human Rights in China, a prominent New York-based rights group, called on China to free all political prisoners to give the Beijing government "a good start" after Deng's death.
Amnesty International said the death of Chinese leader had left in place a "well-oiled machinery for repression", and it urged China to keep up its law reforms.
"The transition from Deng Xiaoping will be a testing time for the future course of human rights in China," the human rights group said in a statement.
Asia-Pacific nations were swift to pay tribute with South Korean President Kim Young-sam saying he was saddened but hoped Seoul's friendly ties with Beijing would be strengthened.
Beijing has declared six days of mourning ending February 25 and the government said no foreign dignitaries would be invited to the funeral in accordance with the country's practice.
